title: Two Banquets and a Walk on the Sea
summary: Herod Antipas, hearing of Jesus, fears that John the Baptist has come back to life, and Matthew tells how Herod had John beheaded at a birthday feast. Jesus withdraws, has compassion on the crowds, and feeds five thousand men, besides women and children, from five loaves and two fish. That night he walks on the sea to his disciples, Peter walks toward him and begins to sink, and those in the boat worship him as the Son of God.
story:
Chapter 13 ended with Jesus rejected in his hometown. Chapter 14 shows a more dangerous rejection: the ruler of Galilee has already killed the prophet who prepared Jesus' way, and now he hears about Jesus. From here to chapter 17 Jesus often withdraws from public places, and the Gospel gives more attention to forming the disciples and to Peter, moving toward Peter's confession in 16:16. The section that begins at 13:54 asks one question in many forms: who is he? Nazareth answers, the carpenter's son; Herod answers, John raised from the dead; the disciples in the boat answer, the Son of God.

The chapter sets two banquets side by side. At Herod's birthday table there is luxury, a rash oath, and a prophet's head on a platter. In a deserted place, at Jesus' table, there is compassion, healing, bread for thousands, and baskets left over. The night on the sea then brings the disciples, for the first time in Matthew, to worship Jesus and confess him as the Son of God, a step beyond the question they asked after the first storm (8:27).
historical:
Herod the tetrarch is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great and his Samaritan wife Malthace, who ruled Galilee and Perea under Rome from 4 BC to AD 39. Matthew gives him his correct title in verse 1 (a tetrarch ruled part of a divided kingdom) and calls him king in verse 9, as people commonly did, though Rome never granted him that title. When he asked the emperor Gaius (Caligula) for it, his nephew Agrippa I accused him, and he was exiled to Lugdunum in Gaul in AD 39, where Herodias chose to follow him (Josephus, Antiquities 18.240-256).

Josephus tells the story of the marriage and of John's death in Antiquities 18. Antipas, visiting a half-brother, fell in love with his wife Herodias, who was also a granddaughter of Herod the Great; she agreed to leave her husband, and Antipas agreed to divorce his first wife, a daughter of the Nabatean king Aretas IV (18.109-110). The law forbade marrying a brother's wife while the brother lived (Leviticus 18:16, 20:21), and Josephus himself says Herodias acted in defiance of the ancestral laws (18.136). He calls John a good man who urged the Jews to practice justice toward one another and piety toward God, and says that Antipas, fearing that John's influence over the crowds might lead to an uprising, sent him in chains to the fortress of Machaerus east of the Dead Sea and killed him there (18.116-119). When Aretas defeated Antipas in battle around AD 36, some Jews saw it as God's punishment for John's death (18.116). Josephus names Herodias's daughter Salome and says she married Philip the tetrarch (18.136-137). Excavations at Machaerus led by Győző Vörös from 2009 have uncovered the Herodian palace where such a banquet could have been held.

Matthew's account is shorter than Mark's (Mark 6:14-29) and differs in one telling way. In Mark, Herodias wants John dead and Herod protects him, fearing him as a righteous man (Mark 6:19-20); in Matthew, Herod himself wants to kill John but fears the people, who regard John as a prophet (verse 5), which is close to the political motive Josephus gives. Both Gospels agree that Herodias's grievance and Herod's oath brought the matter to its end. John's disciples buried him (verse 12). By the middle of the fourth century Christians venerated a tomb of John at Sebaste in Samaria, and the church historian Rufinus records that pagans broke into it and burned the bones in the reign of Julian, around 362.

The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle of Jesus' ministry, apart from the resurrection, told in all four Gospels (Mark 6:30-44, Luke 9:10-17, John 6:1-15). Luke places it near Bethsaida, at the north end of the lake, and John notes that Passover was near, which fits the green grass (verse 19; Mark 6:39). The walk on the sea appears also in Mark 6:45-52 and John 6:16-21, but only Matthew tells of Peter's steps on the water. The Romans divided the night into four watches, so the fourth ran from about three to six in the morning; the Old Testament knows an older reckoning of three (Judges 7:19 speaks of the middle watch). A stadion was about 185 meters, and John puts the boat twenty-five or thirty stadia out, some three or four miles (John 6:19). Gennesaret (verse 34) was the fertile plain on the northwest shore, which Josephus praises for growing walnuts, palms, figs, olives, and grapes side by side (Jewish War 3.516-521).
cultural:
Royal birthday feasts were a Gentile custom that devout Jews regarded warily. Pharaoh's birthday feast ended with one servant restored and another hanged (Genesis 40:20-22), 2 Maccabees 6:7 remembers Jews forced to join the monthly celebration of Antiochus's birthday, and the Mishnah lists the genesia of kings among the pagan festivals near which a Jew should not trade with Gentiles (m. Avodah Zarah 1:3). A girl of the royal family dancing before the guests would have scandalized many Jews. Matthew calls her a korasion, a girl, the word he uses for Jairus's daughter (9:24-25): one girl is raised from death by Jesus, the other is made the instrument of a prophet's death.

Oaths sworn before guests put a ruler's honor at stake. Herod is trapped more by fear of shame than by any sense of right, and Matthew's plural, ‘because of his oaths’, suggests he swore more than once. Matthew's readers had already heard Jesus forbid oaths altogether (5:33-37), and Israel's story knew the horror of a rash vow kept (Judges 11:30-40). Beheading with the sword was a Roman punishment for citizens and was also practiced by Jewish courts: the Mishnah lists slaying by the sword among its four modes of execution and says the head was cut off as the government does it (m. Sanhedrin 7:1, 7:3). The platter (pinax) was a flat serving dish, the kind on which food came to the table. Burying the dead was a sacred duty of family and disciples (Tobit 1:17-18), and John's disciples perform it and then go and tell Jesus.

In the deserted place Jesus follows the pattern of a Jewish meal. The head of the household took bread, spoke a blessing to God (the Mishnah gives its form, blessing God who brings forth bread from the earth, m. Berakhot 6:1), broke it, and distributed it. The people recline on the grass as at a proper meal. The twelve baskets (kophinoi) were stiff wicker baskets that the Roman satirist Juvenal twice associates with Jews (Satires 3.14, 6.542). Counting only the men was an old way of reckoning a crowd; Exodus 12:37 says Israel left Egypt with “about 600,000 men on foot, besides women and children,” and Matthew alone adds the same phrase here and at 15:38, perhaps to recall that exodus crowd.

Fishermen feared the lake at night, and belief in apparitions (phantasmata) was widespread in the ancient world, which explains the disciples' cry. At Gennesaret the sick ask to touch the kraspedon of Jesus' cloak, the tassel the law told Israelite men to wear at the corners of their garments as a reminder of God's commandments (Numbers 15:38-39); a woman had already been healed by touching it (9:20), and Jesus later criticizes those who lengthen theirs for show (23:5).
literary:
The chapter opens with a flashback (verses 3 to 12), one of the few passages in Matthew in which Jesus does not appear, and it is framed by two notices of hearing: Herod hears about Jesus (verse 1), and Jesus hears about John (verse 13). Matthew shortens Mark's story considerably and removes its courtly details (the lords and commanders of Galilee, the girl's hurried return, the soldier of the guard) so that the focus falls on Herod's fear and oath. John's story foreshadows Jesus': a righteous man is arrested, bound, and killed by a ruler who knows better and gives way to pressure, and his disciples bury the body (compare 27:24-26 and 27:57-60). Matthew has already told the reader that the Son of Man will suffer as John did (17:12 makes it explicit).

The verb anachōreō, to withdraw, occurs ten times in Matthew, far more than in any other book, and it marks a pattern: when danger threatens, Jesus withdraws, and his withdrawal becomes the occasion of fresh ministry (2:14, 4:12, 12:15, 14:13, 15:21). Here he withdraws after John's death, the crowds follow on foot, and compassion turns a retreat into a feast. The feeding is told with the four verbs that return at the Last Supper: he took, blessed, broke, and gave (verse 19; 26:26). Matthew leaves out Mark's sheep without a shepherd (he used it at 9:36), the two hundred denarii, and the groups of hundreds and fifties, and adds the women and children.

The sea crossing mirrors the storm in 8:23-27 but moves further. There Jesus was asleep in the boat and the disciples asked what kind of man this was; here he is absent, praying alone on the mountain, comes to them across the water, and they answer the question by worshiping him. Mark ends the same scene with astonishment and hardened hearts (Mark 6:51-52); Matthew ends it with a confession, “Truly You are the Son of God” (verse 33), words that anticipate Peter's confession (16:16) and the centurion's at the cross (27:54). Peter's walk (verses 28 to 31) is Matthew's own material and a small drama in three movements: bold request, faltering fear, and rescue with a rebuke. It is the first of several Peter scenes found only in Matthew (15:15; 16:17-19; 17:24-27), and it prepares for his larger role. Günther Bornkamm's essay on the storm in chapter 8 (1948, in Tradition and Interpretation in Matthew, 1960) argued that Matthew shapes such boat scenes as pictures of discipleship, and many readers see the same design here.

outline.t: Herod fears that John has risen
The death of John the Baptist
Five thousand fed in a desolate place
Peter on the water; the disciples worship

doctrines.note: John is killed not for a crime but for telling a ruler the truth about his marriage (verse 4), and his death comes through a ruler's fear of the crowd, a woman's grudge, and a king's vanity. Matthew presents faithful witness as costly and does not soften its end; the one who prepared Jesus' way also prepares, in his death, the shape of Jesus' own.

The chapter contrasts two kings. Herod, called king though he was only a tetrarch, feasts and kills; Jesus, the true king and shepherd, has compassion, heals, and feeds his people in the wilderness as God fed Israel (verses 14 to 21). His taking, blessing, breaking, and giving anticipate the meal at which he will give himself (26:26).

The same Jesus who withdraws in grief at John's death and prays alone on the mountain (verses 13 and 23) walks on the sea as only God does (Job 9:8) and says, “Take courage! It is I” (verse 27). Matthew sets the human and the divine side by side without explaining how they belong together, and the church confessed at Chalcedon (451) that both are true of one person.

Peter's walk shows faith as trust in Jesus' word (“Come”) and doubt as attention turned from Jesus to the wind (verses 29 and 30). Jesus calls him ‘little faith’, not no faith, and his question, “why did you doubt?” (verse 31), treats doubt as a divided mind in a believer that his hand is quick to rescue.

“Then those who were in the boat worshiped Him” (verse 33). Matthew uses proskuneō thirteen times, often of worship given to Jesus (2:11, 28:9, 28:17), and here the disciples give it for the first time. In a Gospel that insists that God alone is to be worshiped (4:10), Jesus accepts it without correction.

words.note: Splagchnizomai, to have compassion, to be moved in one's inner parts. It occurs 12 times in the New Testament, only in the Synoptic Gospels, five of them in Matthew (9:36, 14:14, 15:32, 18:27, 20:34). The noun splagchna meant the inward organs, thought of as the seat of feeling. In the Gospels the verb is used almost only of Jesus, or of figures in his parables who act as God does (the master in 18:27, the Samaritan, the father of the prodigal). In verse 14 compassion is Jesus' response to a crowd that has interrupted his grief.

Eulogeō, to bless, literally to speak well. It occurs about 41 times in the New Testament. In Jewish practice the blessing at a meal was spoken to God, praising him as the giver of bread, rather than over the food as if to change it. Jesus' blessing in verse 19, spoken looking up to heaven, is that thanksgiving; Matthew uses the same verb at the Last Supper (26:26) and eucharisteō, to give thanks, at the second feeding (15:36) and over the cup (26:27), showing the two words overlap.

Chortazō, to feed until full, to satisfy. It occurs 16 times in the New Testament. It first described fattening animals with fodder (chortos, grass, the word used in verse 19 for the grass the crowd sits on), and came to mean eating one's fill. Everyone ate and was satisfied (verse 20), echoing God's promise to satisfy the hungry (Psalm 107:9) and Jesus' blessing on those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, who “will be filled” (5:6), the same verb.

Phantasma, apparition, ghost. It occurs only twice in the New Testament, in this scene and its parallel (Mark 6:49). The word belongs to the ancient vocabulary of things that appear at night, dreams and phantoms. The disciples' cry shows how far outside their expectation a man walking on the lake lay: the only category they had for it was the uncanny. Jesus answers with his own voice and name.

Egō, I. In verse 27 Jesus says egō eimi, literally ‘I am’, which in context means ‘It is I’. The same words are how the Greek Old Testament renders God's self-naming (Exodus 3:14; Isaiah 43:10, where God says ‘that I am He’). On land they could be ordinary self-identification; spoken by one who treads the waves (Job 9:8) and followed by ‘do not be afraid’, the formula of divine appearances, they carry more than identification.

Oligopistos, of little faith. It occurs five times in the New Testament, four in Matthew (6:30, 8:26, 14:31, 16:8) and once in Luke 12:28, always from Jesus to disciples. It is a Matthean favorite, and its meaning is precise: not unbelief, which Jesus attributes to Nazareth (13:58), but a real faith that falters under pressure. It stands in sharp contrast to the great faith Jesus praises in a Gentile woman in the next chapter (15:28).

Distazō, to doubt, waver, literally to stand two ways. It occurs only twice in the New Testament, both in Matthew: here and in 28:17, where some of the disciples doubt even as they worship the risen Jesus. BDAG glosses it as to have second thoughts or waver. In both places doubt sits side by side with worship in people who have followed Jesus, and in both he comes near to them rather than sending them away.

Proskuneō, to worship, bow down, do obeisance. It occurs about 60 times in the New Testament, 13 in Matthew and 24 in Revelation. It can describe the bow of respect before a king or master (18:26), but in Matthew it gathers around Jesus: the Magi (2:2, 11), a leper (8:2), the Canaanite woman (15:25), the women and the Eleven after the resurrection (28:9, 17). Jesus quotes Deuteronomy against Satan that God alone is to be worshiped (4:10), and here receives worship from his disciples.

christ:
The chapter sets Jesus against the backdrop of Israel's story. As God fed Israel with manna in the wilderness, Jesus feeds a multitude in a desolate place (erēmos, the word for Israel's wilderness), and his disciples' helplessness echoes Moses' cry, “Where can I get meat for all these people?” (Numbers 11:13). Elisha fed a hundred men with twenty loaves of barley bread and there was some left over (2 Kings 4:42-44); Jesus feeds thousands from five loaves and gathers twelve baskets, perhaps one for each tribe of Israel or each of the Twelve. The men counted besides women and children recall the exodus crowd (Exodus 12:37). Psalm 23 pictured the Lord as a shepherd who makes his flock lie down in green pastures and spreads a table for them; here the shepherd-king has the crowd recline on the grass and feeds them. These are patterns rather than predictions, but Matthew means the reader to hear them: the God who fed Israel is feeding his people again.

On the sea the patterns become sharper. The Old Testament describes God as the one who “treads on the waves of the sea” (Job 9:8) and whose “path led through the sea” (Psalm 77:19); Psalm 107 tells of sailors who cried out in a storm and whom the Lord rescued as “He calmed the storm to a whisper” (Psalm 107:29). Peter, sinking, prays like the psalmist, “Save me, O God, for the waters are up to my neck” (Psalm 69:1), and Jesus answers as God answers in Psalm 18:16: “He reached down from on high and took hold of me; He drew me out of deep waters.” Jesus' words “It is I” carry the echo of God's own name, and the disciples respond with the worship due to God alone.

The contrast with Herod completes the picture. The false king feasts and kills the prophet to save face before his guests; the true king, who will himself be bound and handed over by rulers who know better, feeds the hungry and saves the sinking. The meal's words, took, blessed, broke, and gave, anticipate the bread of the Last Supper and his body given for many (26:26), and John's burial by his disciples anticipates Jesus' own. In one chapter Matthew shows who Jesus is by what he does with bread, with the sea, and with a drowning disciple's hand.
interpretation:
The church read the feeding eucharistically from early on. Loaves and fish appear in the art of the Roman catacombs, and the fifth-century mosaic at Tabgha on the northwest shore of the lake, in the Church of the Multiplication, shows a basket of loaves between two fish before the altar. Origen's Commentary on Matthew (book 11, the 240s) read the five loaves as the words of Scripture, answering to the five senses, and the two fish as the word conceived and the word spoken, and he stressed that in Jesus' hands the Word stretches to feed all he wills. John Chrysostom (Homily 49 on Matthew, around 390) drew out the contrast of the chapter's two tables, Herod's lavish feast ending in murder and Christ's plain bread given in compassion.

Peter on the water became a figure of the church and of the believer. Augustine (Sermon 76) calls the sea the present world and Peter a figure of the one church, able to walk only by faith in Christ's command and rescued when he looks at the wind. Giotto's great mosaic in the portico of Old St Peter's in Rome, the Navicella (commissioned by Cardinal Jacopo Stefaneschi around 1298 for the Jubilee of 1300), showed the boat of the church in the storm and Christ lifting Peter from the water; it was destroyed in the rebuilding of the basilica and survives, heavily remade, in the portico of the new St Peter's. John's death became a favorite subject of painters and writers. Beside the works noted on Mark 6, Gustave Moreau's watercolor The Apparition (shown at the Paris Salon of 1876, now in the Musée d'Orsay) shows the dancing girl confronted by a vision of John's head.

The Enlightenment turned the miracles into a problem. H. E. G. Paulus (Das Leben Jesu, 1828) proposed that Jesus' example moved people to share food they had brought and that Jesus was walking by the sea, on the shore, not on it. David Friedrich Strauss (The Life of Jesus, 1835) answered that such explanations distort the texts, and read both stories as myths built from Old Testament models. Rudolf Bultmann (The History of the Synoptic Tradition, German 1921) classed them among the nature miracles, and many later scholars read them as epiphanies, stories that disclose who Jesus is. Redaction critics noticed what Matthew does with Mark: Heinz Joachim Held (in Tradition and Interpretation in Matthew, German 1960) showed how Matthew shapes the miracle stories around faith and little faith, and here turns Mark's hardened hearts into worship. Historians have weighed the account of John's death against Josephus, a question taken up in the second hard question below.

In the liturgy the Revised Common Lectionary reads 14:13-21 and 14:22-33 on Propers 13 and 14 in Year A, and the Roman lectionary reads them on the Eighteenth and Nineteenth Sundays in Ordinary Time. The Roman calendar keeps the memorial of John's beheading on August 29.
text:
Several differences between English Bibles in this chapter come from manuscripts. In verse 3 most manuscripts call Herodias the wife of ‘his brother Philip’, but the Latin Vulgate and a few other witnesses have only ‘his brother’. Some scholars think the name was added from Mark 6:17; most editors keep it. In verse 24 Codex Vaticanus, with some early versions, reads that the boat was “many stadia” distant from the land, the reading modern critical editions print (the BSB's “far from land”). Most other manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read that the boat was ‘in the midst of the sea’, the wording of Mark 6:47, and some textual scholars argue that this majority reading is original. In verse 30 Codex Sinaiticus and the first hand of Codex Vaticanus lack the adjective ‘strong’, so that Peter saw ‘the wind’ rather than “the strength of the wind”; most editors think a scribe's eye skipped from one word ending to the identical ending of the next, and print the adjective. In verse 29 the earliest witnesses read that Peter walked on the water ‘and came toward Jesus’, while later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read ‘to go to Jesus’, which leaves it unclear whether he reached him.

Translation differences are also visible. Verse 8's pinax is ‘a charger’ in the King James Version, an old word for a large flat dish. Verse 22's anagkazō is ‘constrained’ (KJV) or “made” (BSB): Jesus compelled the disciples to leave, perhaps because, as John 6:15 says, the crowd wanted to make him king by force. Verse 27 is ‘Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid’ in the King James Version, and modern versions render the same Greek “Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid.” The note ‘It is I’ cannot show in English that the Greek is egō eimi, ‘I am’, and some versions add a footnote to say so.

teach.big: Jesus is the true king who, unlike Herod, uses his power to feed the hungry and rescue the sinking, and he reveals himself as the Lord of the sea, worthy of worship, even to disciples of little faith.

outline.t: A guilty conscience hears the news about Jesus and sees only the ghost of its own crime.
Speaking truth to power can cost everything, and a ruler who fears the crowd and his guests more than God will kill the righteous to save face.
Jesus grieves, withdraws, and still meets the crowd with compassion; his rest is interrupted by need, and he does not resent it.
Jesus tells his disciples to give what they do not have, takes their little, and gives through their hands more than enough.
Jesus prays while his disciples struggle, then comes to them in the dark over the very thing that threatens them, with his name and his peace.
Faith steps out on Jesus' word and falters when it looks at the wind, but a one-line prayer is enough, and rescue leads to worship.
Those who recognize Jesus bring all their sick to him, and all who touch him are made whole.

teach.pitfalls:
The walk on the water is often preached as a motivational lesson: get out of the boat, take a risk, and you too can walk on water. Peter's request is bold, but the story's climax is not his walk; it is the rescue and the worship of those still in the boat. Teaching it as a technique for success turns a revelation of who Jesus is into a lesson about us, and it can crush people whose faith is weak by implying that sinking is their failure alone. Jesus' rebuke is real, but it comes with his hand already holding Peter.

The feeding is sometimes reduced to the rationalist reading, that the real miracle was everyone sharing hidden lunches; Matthew's wording does not support it. The opposite error makes it only a lesson in generosity or church programs. The disciples do give, but the point is what Jesus does with what they give. The story of John's death should not become a morality tale about dancing or about women as temptresses; the girl is a pawn, and the moral weight falls on Herod, who could have refused. And the fourth watch, the ghost, and the wind should not be allegorized into a map of church history. Let the images echo the Psalms, as Matthew intends, without inventing a code.
teach.pastoral: The death of John will reach people who have suffered for telling the truth: those who confronted abuse, whistleblowers, and anyone who lost standing by refusing to go along. Teach it honestly: faithfulness is sometimes not rewarded in this life, and Matthew does not pretend otherwise, though he shows Jesus grieving and the disciples burying their teacher with love. Jesus' withdrawal after John's death also gives permission to grieve and to seek solitude. Peter's sinking will speak to those who feel their faith is too small, including people with anxiety who fear that their fear itself proves unbelief. Jesus calls it little faith, not no faith, and reaches out his hand ‘immediately’ (verse 31) before he asks his question.

hard.q: Did Jesus really multiply bread and walk on water, or are these stories symbolic?
hard.a:
The skeptical case has two parts. The first is general: David Hume (An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, 1748, section 10) argued that no testimony can make a miracle more probable than the uniform experience against it, and for many modern readers nature miracles are harder to accept than healings, which can be compared with recoveries in other settings. The second is specific. H. E. G. Paulus (1828) proposed natural explanations: the crowd shared food it had brought, and Jesus walked on the shore or in the shallows while the disciples, in the dark, thought he was on the water. David Friedrich Strauss (1835) rejected those explanations as distortions of the text and argued instead that the stories are myths, built by early Christians out of the manna, Elisha's loaves, and the psalms of God treading the sea. Many later critical scholars have followed Strauss in treating the stories as symbolic narratives expressing faith in Jesus, and the dense Old Testament echoes noted above can seem to support that view.

Responses begin with the evidence. The feeding is attested in all four Gospels, including John, whose account most scholars think independent of the other three, and the walk on the sea in three; John's version keeps details (barley loaves, a boy, the crowd's attempt to make Jesus king) that the Synoptics lack. The Evangelists narrate these events as things that happened and that the disciples saw, and Matthew adds Peter's own part. The echoes of manna and of God on the sea do not prove invention; on the Gospels' own account, the God who acted at the exodus was acting again in Jesus, so the events would naturally be told in exodus language. C. S. Lewis (Miracles, 1947) argued that Hume's case assumes what it sets out to prove, since it counts only the experience that excludes miracles as uniform. Craig Keener (Miracles, 2011) has documented how widespread eyewitness claims of extraordinary events are across cultures. Historic Christian faith receives these as real acts of the one through whom all things were made, and grounds that confidence in the resurrection. Readers will weigh the question according to their convictions about whether God acts in the world at all, and it is fair to say that the dispute turns as much on worldview as on the documents.

hard.q: Did Herod want to kill John or not, and can Matthew's account be squared with Josephus?
hard.a:
The objection points to tensions in two directions. Within the Gospels, Matthew says Herod ‘wanted to kill John’ but feared the people (verse 5), yet a few verses later says the king was grieved at the girl's request (verse 9); Mark says instead that Herodias wanted John dead and Herod protected him, knowing him to be righteous (Mark 6:19-20). Critics have taken Matthew's grief as a leftover from Mark that no longer fits his own story. Against Josephus, the differences are larger. Josephus (Antiquities 18.116-119) gives a political motive, fear that John's following might rise in revolt, and says nothing of a banquet, a dance, or an oath; he calls Herodias's first husband Herod rather than Philip and says that Philip the tetrarch married her daughter (18.136-137). Ross Kraemer (Journal of Biblical Literature, 2006) argued that the blame placed on Herodias and her daughter is historically unlikely and serves the Gospel writers' purposes, and many critical scholars regard the banquet scene as a popular tale shaped by Esther and by the story of Ahab, Jezebel, and Elijah.

Responses take several lines. On the internal question, many commentators note that people can want an enemy dead in general and still be distressed when trapped into killing him publicly, against their political judgment and before a crowd that honored him; Matthew's ‘grieved’ may describe Herod's dismay at being cornered rather than affection for John. Matthew's statement that Herod feared the people is in fact close to Josephus's explanation, so Matthew's version stands nearer to Josephus than Mark's does. On the wider question, the Gospels and Josephus agree on the essentials: Antipas imprisoned and executed John, a righteous man with a large following, and the marriage to Herodias was bound up with the affair, since Josephus ties Aretas's war and the popular verdict on it to the divorce and to John's death. Motives can be both personal and political. Harold Hoehner (Herod Antipas, 1972) argued that Herodias's first husband could have been known as Herod Philip, since several Herodian princes bore the family name alongside another, and he defended the general reliability of the Gospel account. Gerd Theissen (The Gospels in Context, 1991) judged that the story reflects popular reports current in Palestine soon after the events, which would explain both its vividness and its imprecision. Readers who hold a high view of Scripture differ on how to resolve the name of the first husband, and the question does not touch the story's point: a prophet died for telling a ruler the truth.

observe: What reasons does Matthew give for Herod's arresting John, for his hesitating to kill him, and for his finally ordering it?
What do the disciples propose when evening comes, and what does Jesus tell them to do instead?
What exactly does Peter ask, what does he do, and what makes him begin to sink?
interpret: How does Matthew's placing of Herod's banquet next to the feeding in the wilderness shape the way we see Jesus' kingship?
What Old Testament pictures of God stand behind Jesus walking on the sea and saying ‘It is I’, and what do they suggest about who he is?
Why do you think Matthew ends the sea story with worship and the confession “Truly You are the Son of God” when Mark ends it with hardened hearts?
apply: Herod did wrong to protect his image before his guests. Where does fear of what others think push you toward choices you know are wrong?
The disciples saw five loaves and a crowd, and Jesus said, “Bring them here to Me.” What small thing might you be holding back from him because it seems too little?
When you are sinking, what would it mean to pray Peter's short prayer and to trust the hand that is already reaching for you?
